# Item banks, test assembly and adaptive testing {#banks-cat}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* describe what an item bank stores and what it is for;
* read a bank's information curve and spot where the bank is thin;
* assemble a fixed form from a bank under content constraints;
* explain, step by step, how a computerized adaptive test (CAT) selects
  items, scores people and decides when to stop;
* judge a CAT design by its precision, test length and item exposure.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[item bank](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#item-bank),
[automated test assembly](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#automated-test-assembly),
[parallel forms](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#parallel-forms),
[computerized adaptive test](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#computerized-adaptive-test),
[multistage test](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#multistage-test),
[exposure](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#exposure).

## The ideas

Once items have been calibrated on a common scale (Chapter \@ref(linking)),
their parameters can be stored in an **item bank** together with their
content codes, usage history and review status. Because the parameters are
on one scale, any selection of items from the bank yields scores on that
scale. That makes two things possible.

**Automated test assembly** (ATA) picks items for a fixed form so that the
form meets a blueprint (for example, ten items from each content area) and
its information curve matches a target: High at a cut score for a licensing
test, flat across the range for a progress test [@vanderlinden2005]. Exact
solutions use mixed-integer programming; simple greedy rules, which add the
best remaining item that still fits the blueprint, often get close.

A **computerized adaptive test** (CAT) goes further and builds a different
test for every person while they take it [@wainer2000]. The loop is:

1. Start with a provisional $\theta$ (often 0).
2. Choose the unused item with the most information at the current
   $\theta$, subject to content and exposure rules.
3. Score the response and update $\theta$ (usually by EAP, which works even
   after one item).
4. Stop when the standard error is small enough or a maximum length is
   reached; otherwise go back to step 2.

A CAT typically reaches the precision of a fixed test with half as many
items or fewer. The price is a bank large enough to cover the whole range,
and **exposure**: Without control, the most informative items are given to
almost everybody and soon become known. A **multistage test** (MST) is a
compromise: People take pre-assembled modules, and the next module depends
on their performance on the last one.

## Example 1: A vocabulary bank and a fixed form

A language-assessment centre has a calibrated bank of 200 vocabulary items
in four areas.

```{r data-banks-cat-1}
# A calibrated 2PL item bank: 200 items, four content areas.
set.seed(1111)
bank <- data.frame(item = sprintf("V%03d", 1:200),
                   area = factor(rep(c("Everyday", "Academic", "Workplace", "Idioms"),
                                     each = 50)),
                   a = rlnorm(200, 0.2, 0.3),
                   b = c(rnorm(50, -0.8, 0.9), rnorm(50, 0.4, 0.9),
                         rnorm(50, 0, 0.9),    rnorm(50, 0.9, 0.7)))
```

The bank's information curve, overall and by area, shows where it can
measure well:

```{r bank-info, fig.cap = "Information of the 200-item vocabulary bank, stacked by content area."}
item_info <- function(a, b, theta) {
  p <- plogis(a * (theta - b)); a^2 * p * (1 - p)
}
grid <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.1)
bank_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(levels(bank$area), function(ar) {
  s <- bank[bank$area == ar, ]
  data.frame(area = ar, theta = grid,
             info = sapply(grid, function(t) sum(item_info(s$a, s$b, t))))
}))
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(bank_info, aes(theta, info, fill = area)) +
  geom_area() +
  labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Bank information", fill = NULL) +
  theme_mirtverse()
```

The bank is rich in the middle and thin at the extremes, especially below
$\theta = -2$ and above $\theta = 2$. Everyday vocabulary covers the low end,
idioms the high end. Item writers should be asked for very easy and very
hard items.

Now a 24-item fixed form with six items from each area, to measure well
between $\theta = -1$ and $\theta = 1$. A greedy assembly adds, one at a
time, the item that adds the most information at the target points, as long
as its area is not yet full:

```{r}
assemble_greedy <- function(bank, length, per_area, targets) {
  chosen <- integer(0)
  while (length(chosen) < length) {
    full <- names(which(table(bank$area[chosen]) >= per_area))
    cand <- setdiff(which(!bank$area %in% full), chosen)
    gain <- sapply(cand, function(i) sum(item_info(bank$a[i], bank$b[i], targets)))
    chosen <- c(chosen, cand[which.max(gain)])
  }
  bank[chosen, ]
}
form <- assemble_greedy(bank, length = 24, per_area = 6, targets = c(-1, 0, 1))
table(form$area)
```

Compared with a random 24-item form that meets the same blueprint:

```{r}
random_form <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(bank, bank$area), function(s) s[sample(50, 6), ]))
se_at <- function(f, theta) 1 / sqrt(sapply(theta, function(t) sum(item_info(f$a, f$b, t))))
round(rbind(assembled = se_at(form, c(-1, 0, 1)),
            random = se_at(random_form, c(-1, 0, 1))), 3)
```

The assembled form measures more precisely at all three target points with
the same length and blueprint. For real programmes, `assemble_forms()` in
the mirtverse [assessment
pipeline](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/assessment-pipeline.html#stage-7)
solves the same problem exactly, builds several parallel forms at once and
handles enemy items (items that must not appear together).

## Example 2: A CAT from scratch

We now write a complete CAT in about 30 lines, using the same bank. The
scoring step computes the EAP estimate on a grid of quadrature points, with a
standard normal prior.

```{r}
quad <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 81)
prior <- dnorm(quad)
eap <- function(a, b, x) {
  like <- sapply(quad, function(t) prod(ifelse(x == 1, plogis(a * (t - b)),
                                                1 - plogis(a * (t - b)))))
  post <- like * prior / sum(like * prior)
  est <- sum(quad * post)
  c(theta = est, se = sqrt(sum((quad - est)^2 * post)))
}
cat_one <- function(true_theta, bank, se_stop = 0.3, max_items = 30, top = 1) {
  used <- integer(0); x <- integer(0); est <- c(theta = 0, se = 1)
  while (length(used) < max_items && est["se"] > se_stop) {
    info <- item_info(bank$a, bank$b, est["theta"]); info[used] <- -Inf
    best <- order(info, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(top)]
    item <- if (top == 1) best else sample(best, 1)   # randomesque exposure control
    used <- c(used, item)
    x <- c(x, rbinom(1, 1, plogis(bank$a[item] * (true_theta - bank$b[item]))))
    est <- eap(bank$a[used], bank$b[used], x)
  }
  list(theta = est[["theta"]], se = est[["se"]], n = length(used), items = used)
}
```

Simulate 300 test takers across the ability range. (To run the CAT on your
own bank, replace `bank` in the data chunk of Example 1; it needs columns
`item`, `area`, `a` and `b`.)

```{r data-banks-cat-2}
# Simulated test takers for the CAT: one true theta per person.
set.seed(1112)
true_theta <- rnorm(300)
```

```{r}
runs <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank)
res <- data.frame(true = true_theta,
                  est = sapply(runs, `[[`, "theta"),
                  se = sapply(runs, `[[`, "se"),
                  n = sapply(runs, `[[`, "n"))
c(mean_length = mean(res$n), rmse = sqrt(mean((res$est - res$true)^2)),
  cor = cor(res$est, res$true))
```

On average the CAT reaches a standard error of 0.3 with far fewer than 30
items. Test length depends on where a person is: In the middle, where the
bank is rich, the CAT stops quickly; at the extremes it runs out of
informative items and goes to the maximum.

```{r cat-length, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Number of items administered by the CAT against true ability."}
ggplot(res, aes(true, n)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "True theta", y = "Items administered") + theme_mirtverse()
```

Exposure is the other side of the coin. With pure maximum-information
selection, a few items are given to a large share of test takers:

```{r}
exposure <- function(runs) {
  table(factor(unlist(lapply(runs, `[[`, "items")), levels = 1:200)) / length(runs)
}
exp_max <- exposure(runs)
sort(round(exp_max, 2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:6]
```

The first item is the same for everybody (the most informative item at
$\theta = 0$), so its exposure is 100%. The **randomesque** method picks at
random among the five most informative items, which spreads exposure at a
small cost in test length:

```{r}
set.seed(1113)
runs_r <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank, top = 5)
exp_r <- exposure(runs_r)
rbind(max_info = c(max_exposure = max(exp_max), mean_length = mean(sapply(runs, `[[`, "n"))),
      randomesque = c(max_exposure = max(exp_r), mean_length = mean(sapply(runs_r, `[[`, "n"))))
```

Content balancing (for example, cycling through the four areas) works the
same way: Restrict the candidate items before choosing the most informative
one. `simulate_cat()` in the assessment pipeline runs this kind of
simulation on a real bank, and the mirtCAT package can deliver an
operational CAT.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Add 20 hard items ($b \sim N(2.2, 0.4)$) to the bank in Example 1 and
   redraw the information curve. What happens to CAT length for the most
   able test takers?
2. Change the stopping rule to $SE < 0.25$. How do mean length and RMSE
   change?
3. Add content balancing to `cat_one()` so that each test has at least four
   items from every area. (Hint: While an area has fewer than four items,
   restrict the candidates to that area.)
4. An admissions officer asks why two applicants got different questions and
   different numbers of questions. Write a short explanation.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
set.seed(1114)
hard <- data.frame(item = sprintf("H%02d", 1:20), area = factor("Idioms", levels(bank$area)),
                   a = rlnorm(20, 0.2, 0.3), b = rnorm(20, 2.2, 0.4))
bank2 <- rbind(bank, hard)
top <- true_theta > 1.5
mean(sapply(lapply(true_theta[top], cat_one, bank = bank2), `[[`, "n"))
mean(res$n[top])

runs25 <- lapply(true_theta, cat_one, bank = bank, se_stop = 0.25)
c(mean_length = mean(sapply(runs25, `[[`, "n")),
  rmse = sqrt(mean((sapply(runs25, `[[`, "theta") - true_theta)^2)))
```

1. The CAT reaches the target precision sooner for the most able test
   takers, because it now has informative items for them.
2. Tests get longer and estimates more precise: Precision costs items.
4. For example: "The test adapts to each applicant: After every answer it
   picks the next question that tells us most about that applicant. Everyone
   is measured on the same scale, and the test stops when it has measured
   each person precisely enough, which takes fewer questions for some people
   than for others."

</details>
